Markets expect steady Fed policy as French debt spread nears 150 basis points
Kevin Warsh Federal Reserve: Rate Hike Shift to December 2026
Federal Reserve Governor Kevin Warsh’s silence on an October rate hike has shifted market expectations toward December, even as French borrowing costs and AI-related credit risks climb. In his October 19, 2026 commentary, Stephen Coltman, Head of Macro at 21shares , highlighted the contrast: easing US Treasury yields, mounting pressure on French debt and widening credit spreads among heavily indebted AI companies.
Markets again expect an October Fed hold, with a possible hike deferred to December.
France’s borrowing premium over Germany is approaching 150 basis points.
Oracle’s credit spreads are moving closer to high-yield levels.
Kevin Warsh leaves Federal Reserve hike expectations pointing to December
Markets expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates at the end of October after Kevin Warsh gave no signal preparing investors for an imminent increase, Coltman wrote. The prospect of a hike has shifted to December 2026 .
Higher-than-expected core inflation in the previous week’s CPI release had prompted markets to price in another increase at the October FOMC meeting. But Warsh did not reinforce that possibility during a public interview at the IMF meetings—his final appearance before the Fed’s quiet period.
Coltman expects no further public remarks from Fed officials before the FOMC meets at the end of October.
French government bonds are moving against other major developed markets, with the 10-year OAT spread over German Bunds approaching 150 basis points , according to Coltman. Since the start of October, the US 10-year Treasury yield has fallen about 20 basis points while French yields have continued rising.
On October 19, France’s 10-year yield jumped more than 10 basis points, while its two-year and 30-year yields rose 6 and 8 basis points, respectively. The CAC 40 fell 1.7% in afternoon trading. French benchmark borrowing costs were touching their highest level since 2002.
Political uncertainty and difficult budget negotiations are compounding the pressure. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s minority government faces obstacles to passing its 2027 budget , which includes a proposed €54 billion in spending cuts. France’s deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP last year; the government is targeting 5%, with a goal of reaching 3% in 2029.
Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin said on October 15 that political uncertainty, rather than a changed fiscal position, was driving higher borrowing costs. Debt servicing costs about €10 billion more annually , he said, complicating consolidation. He nevertheless described France’s financial sector as well capitalized and liquid and said the country had no difficulty finding bond buyers. KBRA’s senior director of sovereigns, Ken Egan, also cited solid underlying demand at the previous week’s auctions.
Coltman takes a more cautious view, describing a sovereign debt crisis that is unlikely to stabilize without first worsening. He considers ECB intervention unlikely unless the stress threatens euro-area bond-market stability. Goldman Sachs senior European equity strategist Sharon Bell similarly said current conditions did not warrant emergency intervention, but disruption to market liquidity would warrant use of the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument.
Coltman also sees Marine Le Pen’s strengthened presidential prospects creating potential structural tensions in Europe in 2027, particularly given her willingness to reduce France’s EU budget contribution unilaterally.
Investors are watching Meta and SpaceX earnings, alongside public information about Anthropic’s IPO, for evidence of AI investment spending , Coltman wrote. At the same time, widening credit spreads are exposing vulnerabilities among heavily indebted AI-related businesses.
Those companies are particularly vulnerable to a slowdown in AI demand, his commentary argues. Oracle stands out: its five-year CDS spreads have widened sharply and now trade closer to those of high-yield borrowers than investment-grade issuers.
Coltman warned that a downgrade of Oracle to speculative grade would make it by far the largest high-yield bond issuer, given its total debt. That scenario would absorb a large share of available capital and potentially crowd out smaller borrowers. His assessment concerns a potential downgrade; the credit-market development he identifies is the sharp widening in Oracle’s CDS spreads.

items.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
items.summary: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing.
items.content:
Image caption, Serhii Beskrestnov said "people have already died" due to lack of warnings about incoming missile attacks
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week , as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."
Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.
Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.
"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."
Figure caption, Watch: Moment Ukrainian soldier lifted to safety by drone
Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.
Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park cafÃ© in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

items.title: Gold Prices Rise Above $4,200 in Futures Trading as Fed Rate Hike Expectations Ease - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Gold Prices Rise Above $4,200 in Futures Trading as Fed Rate Hike Expectations Ease  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Gold Prices Rise Above $4,200 in Futures Trading as Fed Rate Hike Expectations Ease
Gold bars ©Виталий Смолыгин Gold prices advanced on Monday as investors reduced expectations for another US Federal Reserve interest rate increase following comments from Chair Kevin Warsh. US gold futures moved above $4,200 an ounce, while other precious metals also recorded gains.
At 00:51 ET (04:51 GMT), spot gold rose 0.4% to $4,180.29 per ounce, while US gold futures increased 0.5% to $4,200.92.
The gains followed a 0.7% decline in bullion prices during the previous week, when stronger-than-expected US inflation data had reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening.
Investors were also assessing the outlook for the US dollar, government bond yields and demand for gold as a reserve and investment asset.
Warsh Comments Reduce Expectations for Fed Rate Increase
Market expectations for another Federal Reserve interest rate increase shifted following remarks from Chair Kevin Warsh.
Traders reduced the implied probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the central bank's next meeting to below 20%, interpreting Warsh's comments as consistent with keeping interest rates unchanged.
The reassessment followed US inflation figures released the previous week that exceeded market expectations.
Those figures had initially increased expectations of additional monetary tightening and supported the US dollar.
However, Warsh's subsequent remarks interrupted the dollar's advance and prompted investors to reconsider the likelihood of a near-term rate increase.
Higher interest rates can reduce the relative appeal of gold because the metal does not generate interest income.
Other precious metals recorded gains alongside gold during Monday's trading session.
Silver rose 1.3% to $57.7300 per ounce, while platinum increased 1.3% to $1,655.53.
Spot palladium advanced 1.5% to $1,132.74 per ounce.
Meanwhile, the US Dollar Index was broadly unchanged, declining 0.04% to 101.80.
The limited movement in the dollar followed the previous week's increase, which had been supported by expectations of tighter US monetary policy.
Precious metals markets continued to respond to changes in interest rate expectations, currency movements and broader investment demand.
Gold has remained above $4,000 per ounce since August, despite the effects of elevated bond yields and changes in expectations for US interest rates.
The metal previously entered bear-market territory following a decline associated with the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict in late February.
According to the supplied market report, gold remains approximately 20% below its level at the beginning of that conflict.
Demand for assets perceived as offering protection against geopolitical and financial uncertainty has provided some support to prices.
However, the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing assets remains a consideration while government bond yields are elevated.
ANZ Highlights Fiscal Risks and Gold Investment Demand
Analysts at ANZ said concerns about government debt levels and fiscal sustainability were influencing the relationship between bond yields and gold prices.
According to the bank, higher sovereign borrowing costs may increasingly reflect concerns about public finances rather than expectations of stronger economic growth.
In this environment, investors may view gold as a means of diversifying exposure to financial and sovereign debt risks.
ANZ maintained a longer-term positive outlook for the metal while acknowledging that elevated bond yields and a relatively strong US dollar could place pressure on prices in the near term.
The analysts indicated that additional selling could occur before any sustained recovery.
ANZ also identified investment demand from China and reserve diversification by central banks as factors influencing the gold market.
According to the bank, Chinese investors have continued to allocate funds to gold amid subdued conditions in domestic equity and property markets.
Central banks have also increased efforts to diversify reserve holdings and reduce dependence on individual assets.
These sources of demand are relevant to the longer-term outlook for bullion, although their impact on prices will depend on broader financial market conditions.
ANZ expects continued investment and central-bank purchases to contribute to gold demand over the coming years.
ANZ expects gold prices to face limited upside potential in the near term before rising above $5,000 per ounce during 2027.
The forecast reflects the bank's assessment of investment demand, central-bank reserve diversification and fiscal conditions.
However, the projected increase remains dependent on the development of US monetary policy, the dollar and global bond yields.
For now, investors are assessing whether the Federal Reserve will maintain its current interest rate settings at its next meeting.
Gold futures traded above $4,200 per ounce on Monday, while spot prices remained slightly below that level.

items.title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships - The Guardian
items.summary: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships  The Guardian
items.content:
Screengrabs from a social media video show containers and debris floating in the sea after the GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman last week. Composite: Reuters
Screengrabs from a social media video show containers and debris floating in the sea after the GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman last week. Composite: Reuters
People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
A container from the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride floats alongside small motorboats after the ship sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates , sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman , a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ( IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
A satellite image shows containers and items floating in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/Reuters Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Photograph: Reuters On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

items.title: Zelenskyy says Russia hit Ukraine again with no "warning from partners," U.S. delaying "vital supplies" - CBS News
items.summary: Zelenskyy says Russia hit Ukraine again with no "warning from partners," U.S. delaying "vital supplies"  CBS News
items.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Monday that his country had been subjected to another night of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners."
Zelenskyy has accused the U.S. of limiting intelligence, and possibly other assistance to Ukraine amid renewed tension with President Trump, who accused the Ukrainian leader over the weekend of not wanting to end the war. Mr. Trump has significantly softened the U.S. government's policy toward Russia, easing sanctions to allow Russian energy sales in a bid to ease U.S. gas prices.
Zelenskyy says the moves risk emboldening Moscow and enabling it to continue and intensify its four-and-a-half-year, full-scale invasion of Ukraine .
The target of the most recent strikes was energy and other infrastructure, Zelenskyy said , adding that a medical clinic, school, metro station and "ordinary residential buildings" were also hit.
A woman stands amid rubble outside a house damaged by a Russian strike in Dnipro, Ukraine, Oct. 19, 2026.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite technology, to intercept Russian drones. The network is crucial to Ukrainian forces as it enables them to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones and other weapons.
The Trump administration has denied making any changes to the intelligence it shares with Ukraine, or deliberately slowing down Starshield data.
Asked Saturday if the U.S. government was responsible for the change in Starlink service in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate … we have nothing to do with that."
"The United States — nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before," he said, without elaborating on what he meant by "it sort of happened."
Denys Sienik, Ukraine's chargé d'affaires and current top diplomat in the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or Musk's SpaceX to inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X , adding that there had also been "delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War."
He did not expound on his assertion that the Pentagon was delaying shipments of supplies.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is seen during an interview at his office in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 18, 2026.
The Ukrainian leader issued the statement amid an increasingly terse exchange of accusations with President Trump who, over the weekend, accused Zelenskyy of not wanting the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion to end.
In a Truth Social post , Mr. Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump argued.
The U.S. president has over the last month walked back sanctions on Russia — that had support from a majority of Republicans and Democrats — that were intended to increase financial pressure on Moscow over its assault on Ukraine.
"Ukraine never wanted this war," Zelenskyy said in another statement shared Monday on social media. "We took positively literally EVERY attempt of partners to end this war with dignity."
Just over a week ago Mr. Trump declared in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," which would mean a halt to attacks on the other country's energy infrastructure. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to any such deal, and within hours Ukrainian authorities reported new Russian attacks on refineries.
A worker sweeps up rubbish outside the Chalet Ice Arena, which was damaged in a Russian ballistic missile attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 19, 2026, amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said "again and again Russia's answers" to efforts at diplomacy were new attacks.
"Putin does not want the end of this war, or even any de-escalation steps," he said, adding: "It is very important to call things by their names. Call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine protect lives. When the supply of missiles to Ukrainian air defense is blocked, and Russia receives a weakening or postponement of sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality from partners. In reality, the war continues, and continues only because of Russian strikes — the Russian desire to prolong this war."
The Kremlin, meanwhile, has attempted to frame Russia as a willing partner in peace efforts.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Moscow values U.S. mediation efforts, but that reaching agreements without the participation of representatives from Kyiv is impossible. There have been direct talks, mediated by the U.S., between Ukraine and Russia, but so far the meetings have yielded little more than prisoner swaps, not ceasefires.
The Wall Street Journal first reported Sunday evening that Putin had proposed a meeting between U.S., Chinese and Russian officials to discuss solutions to the Ukraine war, but without a seat for Ukraine at the negotiating table. The newspaper said he proposed the idea for a summit during a call with Mr. Trump on Oct. 9.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Monday in a post on X that "a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."

Putin reportedly suggests summit with Trump, Xi about Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal reported Vladimir Putin had reportedly suggested a summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping for a deal to end the Ukraine war.
The summit is not confirmed, but if it takes place will not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The report comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report.
The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.
"The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
Over the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace , while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."
The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.
In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.
Ukraine's First Deputy Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Monday that Kyiv still hoped to retain Washington's support despite the growing tensions.
Asked whether the Trump administration was abandoning Ukraine and siding with Russia, Derkach said he did not believe the U.S. was abandoning Kyiv, but stressed that Ukraine hoped Washington would continue helping it or at least "stay in the middle."
"That's most important for us actually, not to lose the support of the U.S.," he said.
Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine's transport infrastructure, including road border crossings, railways and shipping routes, Derkach said.
It comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up global diesel prices.
Despite an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11, Russia continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Kyiv paused its attacks for three days before resuming them last Thursday, citing continued Russian strikes.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.
On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."
"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."
Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St. Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink. Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."
Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces, after Reuters reported on Thursday that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from someone inside the White House, citing two U.S. officials.

items.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says - The Guardian
items.summary: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says  The Guardian
items.content:
Workers repair railway tracks at a metro station hit by an overnight Russian missile strike on Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
Workers repair railway tracks at a metro station hit by an overnight Russian missile strike on Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
Ukrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in continuing row with Trump over apparent support for Moscow
Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.
Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.
“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.
“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.
On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia , telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.
The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war , and probably never did.”
Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We ‌would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If ‌President Xi wants to have it, I’d ​have it.”
For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.
Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”
US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.
The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink , the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.
Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.
The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.
Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.
Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.
Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.
Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

items.title: Amazon challenges Nvidia’s software advantage with new tool for its own AI chips - GeekWire
items.summary: Amazon challenges Nvidia’s software advantage with new tool for its own AI chips  GeekWire
items.content:
by Todd Bishop on Oct 19, 2026 at 6:25 am October 19, 2026 at 6:28 am
Amazon’s TorchNeuron sits between PyTorch and the company’s Trainium chips, supporting developers’ existing code. (Amazon Image)
A new software tool from Amazon aims to make switching from Nvidia to the company’s own AI chips about as simple as changing a setting.
The software, dubbed TorchNeuron, runs code written in PyTorch, the open-source framework used by many AI developers, on Amazon’s Trainium chips. It has been in private beta since late last year, and Amazon said Monday that it’s opening the software to all developers as a public beta .
Until now, developers who wanted to run PyTorch code on Trainium had to modify it to call programming interfaces specific to Amazon’s chips, said Colin Brace , vice president of technology software at Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip-design unit. With TorchNeuron, the same code runs after a basic configuration change.
“If you know PyTorch, then you know Trainium,” Brace said in an interview.
Nvidia dominates the market for AI chips, partly because much of the industry’s AI software was built around its CUDA platform. Adapting that code to other hardware can take months of engineering work. That has made many companies reluctant to switch, even as Amazon, Google and others have developed their own chips.
TorchNeuron is part of a broader push by tech giants to loosen Nvidia’s grip on AI computing, even as they remain among its biggest customers.
Google, which has started selling its TPU chips directly to some outside customers, is working on TorchTPU , a similar project to run PyTorch natively on those chips. Google detailed the effort in April, saying the goal is to let developers move existing PyTorch code to TPUs with minimal changes.
Microsoft said last week that it plans to run most of its AI services on its homegrown Maia chips rather than Nvidia hardware.
Amazon is reportedly in talks to acquire Decart , a startup that makes software to help developers move AI models built for Nvidia chips to alternatives such as Trainium, in a deal that could value it at about $7 billion. Decart already runs its own AI models on Trainium, and Nvidia is an investor in the startup.
Asked about Amazon’s relationship with Nvidia, Brace said the company has “always been about choice,” pointing to another high-profile example: AWS offers Intel processors alongside its own Graviton chips.
Amazon plans to release TorchNeuron as open-source software on Tuesday in conjunction with the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, Calif.
Trainium’s biggest users so far are AI labs with close financial ties to Amazon. Anthropic, in which Amazon has invested billions , uses the chips to train and run its Claude models. OpenAI agreed in February to use 2 gigawatts of Trainium capacity as part of a deal in which Amazon is investing $50 billion in the company.
Brace said Amazon’s goal has always been wide use of the chips, calling TorchNeuron “an accelerant” along those lines.
Amazon’s chip business traces back to its 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs , an Israeli chipmaker, for a reported $350 million. The Annapurna team went on to design Trainium as well as Amazon’s Graviton processors.
In his annual shareholder letter in April, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy wrote that the company’s chip business, including Trainium and Graviton, had an annual revenue run rate of more than $20 billion. He estimated that figure would be about $50 billion if the chips were sold to AWS and other customers by a standalone chip business.
“There’s so much demand for our chips that it’s quite possible we’ll sell racks of them to third parties in the future,” he wrote.
More than 30 companies and internal Amazon teams have been using TorchNeuron during the private beta. Deepgram, a San Francisco startup that makes speech AI, says its benchmarks showed Trainium processing about 60% more audio per dollar than its existing GPU setup. The company now runs Trainium in production, Brace said.
Inside Amazon, the Prime Video team used TorchNeuron to build Prime 360 , an AI system that reconstructs NBA plays in 3D so viewers can watch replays from angles a traditional camera can’t capture. The feature, which runs on Trainium, will appear on select Prime Video broadcasts this NBA season.
To make sure TorchNeuron works with the huge variety of AI models that developers build, Amazon tests it every night against more than 100,000 models from Hugging Face, the popular online hub for open-source AI, Brace said.
Brace said the timing of the project reflects changes in PyTorch itself. The framework has matured, and its maintainers have been working to make it less dependent on any one kind of hardware.
Amazon has contributed to that effort, removing code that tied PyTorch to specific chips. Newer versions of PyTorch can detect which hardware they’re running on, he said, so in some cases developers don’t need to change their code at all.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Technology Earnings as Oil Prices Decline: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Trading floor of the New York stock exchange ©Carol M. Highsmith Archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division US stock futures moved higher on Monday as investors prepared for quarterly earnings from major technology companies amid concerns about artificial intelligence investment and financing conditions. Oil prices declined following US President Donald Trump's decision to waive certain sanctions on Russia, while Chinese economic data showed an acceleration in third-quarter growth.
Futures linked to the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 advanced in early trading, following declines in the main Wall Street indices on Friday.
Investors were also assessing preliminary financial results from Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), whose shares declined despite forecasts of substantial revenue growth and a return to profitability.
US Futures Advance Following Technology Sector Declines
At 03:06 ET (07:06 GMT), Dow Jones futures had risen 215 points, or 0.4%, while S&P 500 futures gained 53 points, or 0.7%.
Nasdaq 100 futures increased 384 points, equivalent to 1.3%.
The gains followed a decline in US equities on Friday, when concerns about financing requirements and valuations across the artificial intelligence sector affected technology stocks.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge described investor sentiment towards AI-related equities as "considerably darker".
The firm highlighted concerns about the sustainability of debt and equity issuance used to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure.
Media reports indicating that quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI model, remained substantial but had slowed compared with the preceding quarter also contributed to investor attention on the sector.
Vital Knowledge analysts said: "While many stocks are still above their summer lows, the psychology towards the group seems worse than it was in June and July, due in large part to the dramatic worsening in certain pockets of the AI credit market."
Analysts at ING also examined the potential implications of technology market volatility for the US dollar.
The bank said the dollar "could be a laggard in further stock market instability", although it did not anticipate an imminent substantial decline in the currency.
The assessment reflects concerns that changes in investor positioning towards AI-related assets could affect other financial markets.
Investors are continuing to evaluate the financing requirements of major technology companies and the potential relationship between infrastructure expenditure, revenue growth and future profitability.
Quarterly earnings from major US technology companies will be a focus during the week, particularly as investors assess spending on artificial intelligence.
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to report its results after the US market close on Wednesday.
The company has expanded its AI activities following the September launch of its Muse model, which reportedly attracted millions of downloads.
The technology includes services designed to assist users with travel bookings and small-business tasks.
Meta has also released an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
Investors will be examining Meta's financial performance and management commentary on AI investment, capital expenditure and the commercial development of its technology.
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) is also scheduled to publish quarterly results after Wednesday's closing bell.
The company recently attracted attention following a live demonstration in which a booster-powered vehicle completed a controlled landing.
Both earnings announcements come during a period of increased scrutiny of technology companies' investment programmes and growth expectations.
Oil Prices Fall Following US Decision on Russian Sanctions
Crude oil prices declined on Monday after President Donald Trump issued an executive order suspending numerous sanctions on Russia shortly before their scheduled implementation.
The administration also waived proposed tariffs on countries importing Russian oil.
At 03:56 ET, Brent crude futures fell 2.6% to $106.97 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures declined 2.0% to $99.36 per barrel.
The declines followed a gain of nearly 5% in crude prices during the previous week, when concerns about supply disruptions, particularly in the Middle East, supported the market.
The US measures raised expectations that additional Russian crude could remain available to international buyers.
Trump subsequently indicated on social media that maintaining Russia's participation in negotiations was among the considerations behind his approach to efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Earlier, the president had said that no final decision had been made, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the administration could take up to 60 days to assess the economic effects of the waivers.
Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies forecast a substantial increase in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, citing demand associated with artificial intelligence and higher memory chip prices.
In a preliminary earnings estimate, CXMT projected revenue of between 265 billion yuan and 270 billion yuan, equivalent to approximately $39.6 billion to $40.4 billion.
The forecast compares with revenue of 32.08 billion yuan in the corresponding period of 2025, representing an increase of more than eight times.
The company also expects net profit attributable to shareholders of between 131 billion yuan and 132.5 billion yuan.
This would represent a reversal from the net loss of 5.28 billion yuan recorded in the first nine months of the previous year.
Despite the projected improvement in financial performance, CXMT shares declined.
The share price movement came amid heightened investor expectations for companies benefiting from demand for AI-related semiconductor products.
China's Third-Quarter GDP Growth Accelerates to 4.5%
China's economy expanded faster than expected in the third quarter of 2026, supported by exports and demand associated with artificial intelligence.
Data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed gross domestic product increased 4.5% year on year in the three months ended September 30.
The result exceeded economists' expectations for 4.4% growth and represented an acceleration from the 4.3% annual increase recorded in the preceding quarter.
On a quarter-on-quarter basis, GDP grew 1.2%, compared with forecasts of 1.1% and growth of 0.9% in the second quarter.
For the first nine months of 2026, China's economy expanded by 4.6%.
The figures place growth within the government's previously stated annual target range of 4.5% to 5%.
Investors Monitor Earnings, Energy Markets and Chinese Growth
Financial markets began the week with gains in US stock futures, lower crude oil prices and further developments in the technology sector.
The upcoming earnings announcements from Meta and Tesla will provide additional information about corporate performance and investment plans.
At the same time, changes to US sanctions on Russia are influencing expectations for global oil supply, while China's economic data and CXMT's preliminary results provide further indications of activity in the Chinese economy and semiconductor industry.

Image caption, Monfils and Svitolina played in the mixed doubles together at this year's US Open and reached the semi-finals
Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player GaÃ«l Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.
The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".
"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.
She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".
"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.
It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.
"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.
Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."
The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.
Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.

items.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
items.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.
Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.
He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.
The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.
The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.
There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.
If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.
Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.
Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."
He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.
Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.
Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.
Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.
Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.
"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.
Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

Wall Street Futures Rise as Technology Stocks Recover and Oil Prices Ease: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Technology network ©Adobe Stock Images US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Monday, with technology shares expected to recover some of the losses recorded during the previous session. A decline in crude oil prices also contributed to the improvement in market sentiment.
Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 1.3%, indicating potential gains in technology stocks following Friday's decline, which left the Nasdaq Composite at its lowest closing level in a month.
Investors appeared to be reassessing technology valuations after recent selling, partly driven by concerns about the scale of debt-financed investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Oil prices also retreated after several sessions of increases. The decline followed an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump waiving key provisions of recently introduced sanctions against Russia. Trump said the decision was in the national interest of the United States.
The easing in crude prices followed a period of volatility linked to geopolitical developments, including renewed Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and uncertainty surrounding a reported energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
US crude oil futures had previously risen above $100 per barrel for the first time in a month.
US equities fell on Friday after recovering from an earlier decline to finish Thursday's session mostly higher.
The Nasdaq Composite lost 572.99 points, or 2.1%, to close at 26,140.03. The S&P 500 declined 84.62 points, or 1.1%, to 7,659.44, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.3%, to 52,002.41.
For the week, the Nasdaq declined 4.5% and the S&P 500 lost 2%. The Dow, however, gained 0.7%.
Technology stocks accounted for a significant portion of Friday's selling, with investors continuing to assess the financing requirements and potential returns associated with artificial intelligence infrastructure investment.
Computer hardware companies recorded some of the largest declines. The NYSE Arca Computer Hardware Index fell 5.4%, reaching its lowest closing level in two months.
Semiconductor, networking and software shares also declined, contributing to the Nasdaq's losses.
Outside the technology sector, airline stocks came under pressure as higher crude oil prices increased attention on fuel costs.
The NYSE Arca Airline Index fell 3.2% during Friday's session.
Brokerage and biotechnology shares also recorded declines, while energy companies advanced alongside crude oil prices.
Oil market movements reflected uncertainty surrounding supply conditions, particularly following developments in the Strait of Hormuz and the reported deterioration of the Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire.
The subsequent decline in crude oil futures on Monday provided a different backdrop for equity trading ahead of the US market opening.
On the economic front, Federal Reserve data showed that US industrial production increased by 0.7% in September, exceeding economists' expectations of a 0.4% rise.
The August figure was revised to an increase of 0.1%, compared with the previously reported unchanged reading.
The September result indicated an acceleration in industrial activity compared with the previous month.
The report provided additional information on US economic conditions as investors assessed the outlook for growth, inflation and monetary policy.
Market attention remained focused on the potential recovery in technology shares, movements in energy prices and the implications of geopolitical developments for financial markets.

Third Wheel: Microsoft’s AI Chips Are “Nowhere Close” to NVIDIA or Google per Analyst
Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 AI chip on Monday and plans to scale its Maia chips to multi-gigawatt deployments starting next calendar year.
Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh said Microsoft's chips are "nowhere close" to Google's TPUs or NVIDIA, which puts Alphabet ahead in the custom-chip race.
Microsoft's capital expenditures reached $116 billion in the year ended June 2026, nearly 5x the level four years earlier, while NVIDIA has kept a gross margin above 70% for three straight fiscal years.
Microsoft measures Maia against GPU-based systems, so the real test is how its spending and its NVIDIA orders look once the larger rollout starts next year.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) just made what CEO Satya Nadella calls "our biggest bet yet on our own silicon."
On Monday, Nadella posted on X that Microsoft will scale its Maia chips "to multi-gigawatt deployments" starting next calendar year, "making it the primary inference system for our own product and services." He said the new Maia 300 "delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems."
Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh was less impressed. Asked on Monday's episode of a Bloomberg Intelligence podcast whether Maia threatens NVIDIA, he said Microsoft and its peers "are still way behind when it comes to incorporating their own chips in the tech stack."
Then he added: "they're nowhere close to where Google is at with its TPUs or where NVIDIA is at."
That leaves Microsoft as the third wheel in its own chip story.
Singh's point is that Alphabet ( GOOG ) has already done what Microsoft is only now scaling up. He called Google's vertical integration "the playbook to emulate." He noted that Google is on its eighth or ninth generation of TPUs, and now makes separate chips for training and for inference.
Google also rents its TPUs to outside customers, so the chips earn money on top of serving Google's own products.
Meanwhile, Alphabet's operating margin rose from 26.5% in 2022 to 32.0% in 2025, during its heavy spending on AI.
Alphabet (GOOG): operating (EBIT) margin (%), fiscal 2021–2025 ( TIKR )
How much of that comes from TPUs can't be separated out from the outside, and the ad business does a lot of the work. Still, it's the margin trend you'd expect from a company that owns more of its own AI stack.
The reason to build your own chips is to stop paying NVIDIA's prices. NVIDIA's gross margin has topped 70% in each of its last three fiscal years, which is rich for a hardware maker.
Nvidia (NVDA): gross margin (%), fiscal 2022–2026 (years to January) ( TIKR )
Microsoft is pouring money into data centers at a pace that makes that markup hard to ignore. Its capital expenditures climbed from $23.9 billion in the year ended June 2022 to $116 billion in the year ended June 2026.
Microsoft (MSFT): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2022–2026 (years to June) ( TIKR )
Moving even a small share of that budget from NVIDIA's GPUs to Maia would save real money. That's why Singh says Microsoft has to keep at it. If it doesn't, he said, "they'll be reliant on NVIDIA for the foreseeable future."
To be fair to Microsoft, Maia is real. Nadella says Maia 200 is already deployed across the US, Europe, and Australia, "delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot." Microsoft says the chip also runs OpenAI's models and its own MAI models.
Look at what those gains are measured against, though. Both the 1.7x and the 40% compare Maia with "leading GPU-based systems," so the benchmark is NVIDIA's hardware. None of Microsoft's figures compares Maia with a TPU, and Google's TPUs are the bar Singh sets. The 1.7x is also an "up to" figure, measured in Microsoft's own apps.
Nadella's post also says Microsoft will keep "bring[ing] the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet." I read that as a promise to keep buying other companies' chips, NVIDIA's included.
On the evidence, Singh's call holds up. Maia should trim Microsoft's NVIDIA bill over time. But Google is several chip generations ahead and already rents its TPUs to others, so Alphabet leads the custom-chip race today. Microsoft is still catching up.
Of course, Maia's multi-gigawatt rollout only starts next calendar year. Microsoft's capital spending in the quarters after that will show whether the gap is closing faster than Singh expects.

Trump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu for reelection Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
FILE - President Donald Trump listens as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla.
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump's popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Elections in Israel will be a verdict on Netanyahu's handling of October 7
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
"Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together," Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. "Together we will complete the mission!"
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump's ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries' key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
Trump confirms calling Netanyahu 'crazy,' says they still get along
In his post, Trump again threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran "unless they change their ways, rapidly," but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself."
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, "I'm not involved in politics anymore," despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first
Trump criticized Israel's decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu "crazy." Trump also said that he was "a little bit perturbed" as Israel's fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump's latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration's call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.
