Nvidia vs. TSMC: Which Business Depends Less on Picking the Winning AI Chip?
Nvidia and TSMC both appear in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade , but they offer different answers to a long-term problem: what happens if the winning AI-chip architecture changes? Owning a manufacturer can spread that technology bet, although it introduces a different set of concentrated risks. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) sells a computing platform built around its chips, networking and software. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM ) manufactures customers' designs. They are alternative ways to own AI-computing growth, not direct substitutes in the supply chain.
Nvidia vs. TSMC: Which Business Depends Less on Picking the Winning AI Chip? Courtesy of NVIDIA
TSMC's advantage is conditional neutrality: it can earn manufacturing revenue from competing customers when their designs use its processes. A shift toward custom accelerators could therefore leave manufacturing demand intact even if it pressures a merchant-chip supplier. The inference depends on where the replacement chips are made; it is not proof that TSMC captures every design win.
Its third-quarter results reported 79% of wafer revenue from technologies at seven nanometers and below. Two-nanometer products contributed 8%, demonstrating an ongoing process transition. Maintaining that position requires yields, reliable delivery and expensive capacity. Our TSMC-ASML expansion comparison explains how much cash ownership of the factories can consume.
Nvidia's opposing strength is that customers buy usable computing, not merely transistor capacity. Its ecosystem and system integration can preserve demand even when another chip looks attractive on an isolated specification. The risk is that customers develop enough software and custom hardware to reduce what they pay for that integration.
Diversification changes the risk rather than removing it
Nvidia's latest quarter generated $89 billion of data-center revenue out of $96.22 billion total, about 92.5%. That concentration creates powerful exposure to infrastructure spending. A broad customer roster would not eliminate a shared customer-capital-spending shock.
TSMC reported a 58.7% operating margin in its latest quarter, but a foundry's customer diversity does not diversify away factory location or utilization. If demand falls across designers, the manufacturer still owns the capacity. Our geographic-risk comparison examines why changing the point of entry into the chip supply chain does not automatically remove Taiwan exposure.
Using October 16 prices, Nvidia's equity value was about 41 times trailing cash after capital expenditure. The equity value implied by TSMC's U.S. depositary-share price was about 47 times, using five ordinary shares per depositary share. These historical cash multiples include different investment cycles; they are not evidence that the foundry is automatically the cheaper route.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders increased to 285 from 275 for Nvidia and to 249 from 234 for TSMC. Fisher added 3% to Nvidia shares, and Fisher increased TSMC shares 2%. Nvidia's September 30 short interest was 1.35% of float.
TSMC offers less dependence on a single merchant-computing architecture, provided it retains the manufacturing work. Nvidia offers greater exposure to the value of an integrated platform. The choice turns on whether an investor is more confident in platform economics or manufacturing leadership, while separately accounting for valuation and geography.
While we acknowledge the potential of NVDA and TSM as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. A Repeat Of ‘Black Monday' Would Send The S&P 500 Down More Than 1,500 Points And Wipe Out More Than $13 Trillion In Stock Market Value
Thirty-nine years after a single October Monday vaporized trillions and paralyzed markets worldwide, analysts are drawing uncomfortable parallels between 1987 and today's AI-fueled rally, and the math behind a repeat scenario is sobering.
A dramatic red, burning trend line on a financial chart symbolizes a steep market decline, reflecting the volatility and potential for significant losses discussed in relation to events like 'Black Monday'. © Travis Wolfe / Shutterstock.com
The benchmark S&P 500 is still up 11.9% this year, but Wall Street marks Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, the 39th anniversary of the 1987 crash , after a rough week.
On that day in 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average suffered its largest one-day percentage drop ever, a 22.6% collapse. But applying Black Monday ‘s 20.47% S&P 500 decline to Friday's close would erase about 1,568 points by our arithmetic, leaving the index near 6,092. The Dow's 22.61% drop would remove about 11,750 points, leaving it near 40,245.
This is simple arithmetic on Friday's closes and is not meant as a prediction.
In dollars, the same S&P 500 decline applied to the index's $68.45 trillion market cap at the end of the third quarter, equals about $14.0 trillion.
Friday rattled investors, the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659.44, the Dow slid 0.3% to 52,002.41 and the technology-packed Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.1% to 26,140.03. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq logged their worst week since June, led by chip stock. The Dow and Nasdaq remain up 8.2% and 12.5% this year.
The Dow fell 3.81% on Oct. 14, 2.39% on Oct. 15 and 4.6% on Oct. 16. On Oct. 19, it opened at 2,246.74 and closed at 1,738.74, a 508-point plunge. The S&P 500 sank 20.47%, the Wilshire 5000 dropped 18% and estimated worldwide losses reached $1.71 trillion. Systems struggled: 195 of 2,257 NYSE-listed stocks faced delays or halts, and 95 S&P 500 stocks opened late while futures opened on time.
Possible triggers included a House bill to curb tax benefits for mergers and leveraged buyouts and a higher-than-expected trade deficit released Oct. 14. Many saw stocks as overvalued, while trade and budget deficits, rising interest rates and a falling dollar added to concern. Portfolio insurance (computer-driven selling of index futures), index arbitrage through program trading, weekend mutual fund redemptions and early selling ahead of the expected Monday drop amplified the rout. The 1988 Brady Report found margin calls ran about ten times their average size and judged portfolio insurance a possible contributing factor rather than the initial trigger.
On Oct. 20, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said the Fed "affirmed today its readiness to serve as a source of liquidity." It injected $17 billion that day, and the federal funds rate fell about half a percentage point. The S&P 500 bottomed at 230.30 in November 1987, down 31.6% from its Aug. 25 high of 336.77, and regained that high on July 26, 1989.
The NYSE adopted trading curbs in 1988, and regulators later created market-wide circuit breakers, used during the 2020 crash. Under the SEC's investor guidance , a single-day S&P 500 decline of 7% or 13% from the prior close before 3:25 p.m. ET halts trading for 15 minutes, with no halt at or after 3:25 p.m. A 20% decline at any time halts trading for the rest of the day. On Friday's close, those levels sit near 7,123, 6,664 and 6,128, so a 1987-size drop would breach the third. Losses can still pile up until each level is hit.
Michael Burry, whose bearish calls we have examined before , wrote in a Substack post, "I continue to believe it is possible the markets are near a major top." He pointed to leverage built by volatility-targeting and momentum strategies in a low-volatility market and compared it with the lead-up to Oct. 19, 1987. He is bearish on AI-linked stocks and reportedly holds short positions including NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) and Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ), though he has warned short selling is high-risk.
According to Bloomberg on Oct. 9, Joachim Klement of Panmure Liberum says the AI bubble will burst in 2027 or 2028, with his target implying 36% downside for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027. He is the most bearish of eight strategists Bloomberg tracks; the other seven average about 14% upside. He does not recommend selling now.
The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report on Oct. 13 warned a sharp correction in AI stocks could spread through global markets, citing elevated AI valuations, higher government borrowing costs and a major cyberattack as possible catalysts. "Resilience is not safety," said the IMF's Athanasios Vamvakidis. Temasek CIO Rohit Sipahimalani calls a reversal of the AI trade a key risk.
Fund manager Adrian Day says some conditions mirror 1987, including higher rates, dollar and deficit concerns and an AI sector many consider overvalued, though yields aren't yet high enough to pull large sums out of stocks. Jim Paulsen, on the Excess Returns podcast Oct. 15, highlighted complacency and a possible "fairly nasty correction," particularly in new-era stocks, without a recession or all-out bear market. Riding a mania is one thing; knowing when to leave is the harder half, and we covered both in a free bubble survivor's handbook .
Citigroup ( NYSE:C ) strategists say solid 2027 earnings can support further gains, and Jefferies ( NYSE:JEF ) projects the S&P 500 could reach 9,000 by the end of 2027, per Invezz. The market has historically survived its worst days.

US Stock Futures Advance as Nasdaq 100 Signals Recovery Following Technology Sell-Off: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Technology network ©Adobe Stock Images US equity futures moved higher on Monday, suggesting that Wall Street could recover some of the losses recorded at the end of the previous week, as technology stocks attracted renewed interest and crude oil prices declined.
Nasdaq 100 futures rose 1.3% ahead of the opening bell, following a session in which technology shares accounted for a substantial portion of the broader market's losses.
The expected recovery followed Friday's decline, which pushed the Nasdaq Composite to its lowest closing level in a month.
Market participants were reassessing technology shares after recent selling linked to concerns about borrowing to finance artificial intelligence infrastructure and the potential returns from those investments.
A retreat in crude oil futures also provided a different backdrop for trading after prices had increased over several sessions.
The decline followed an executive order signed by President Donald Trump waiving key provisions of newly introduced sanctions against Russia. Trump said the decision was justified by US national interests.
Oil markets had previously responded to renewed Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and indications that a reported energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine was no longer holding.
US crude oil futures had risen above $100 a barrel for the first time in a month before retreating on Monday.
Technology Sector Losses Push Nasdaq to One-Month Low
US stocks ended Friday's session lower, reversing the predominantly positive finish recorded on Thursday.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 572.99 points, or 2.1%, to 26,140.03, while the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points, or 1.1%, to 7,659.44.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average recorded a smaller decline, losing 175.28 points, or 0.3%, to close at 52,002.41.
Over the full trading week, the Nasdaq dropped 4.5% and the S&P 500 declined 2%. The Dow gained 0.7%, reflecting differences in performance between the major indices.
Technology shares were particularly affected by concerns surrounding capital expenditure on artificial intelligence infrastructure, including the use of debt to finance development.
Computer hardware stocks recorded some of the largest losses, with the NYSE Arca Computer Hardware Index falling 5.4% to its lowest closing level in two months.
Shares in semiconductor manufacturers, networking equipment providers and software companies also declined.
The losses across these industries contributed to the Nasdaq's weekly decline and provided the context for Monday's anticipated recovery.
Oil Price Movements Affect Airlines and Energy Stocks
The increase in crude oil prices during the previous week affected several sectors of the US equity market.
Airline shares declined as investors assessed the potential effect of higher fuel prices on operating costs.
Brokerage and biotechnology stocks also moved lower, while energy shares advanced alongside crude oil futures.
Oil prices had risen amid uncertainty surrounding international supply routes and geopolitical developments.
Renewed attacks by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, an important passage for global energy shipments, added to concerns about potential supply disruptions.
Uncertainty surrounding a reported energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine also contributed to fluctuations in crude prices.
Monday's decline in oil futures followed the US decision to waive certain sanctions provisions affecting Russia.
The change in energy prices was among the factors influencing equity futures before the start of regular trading.
Federal Reserve Reports 0.7% Increase in Industrial Production
Investors also considered US economic data showing that industrial production increased more than expected in September.
According to the Federal Reserve, industrial output rose 0.7% during the month, compared with economists' forecasts for a 0.4% increase.
The August reading was revised to a gain of 0.1%, replacing the previously reported unchanged figure.
The September increase therefore represented an acceleration from the previous month's revised growth rate.
Industrial production provides an indication of activity across manufacturing, mining and utilities and is one of the measures used to assess economic conditions.
The figures added to the information available to investors as they evaluated the outlook for US growth and monetary policy.
Investors Monitor Technology Shares and Energy Markets
Monday's higher index futures suggested a possible change in direction following the previous week's losses, particularly among technology companies.
Nasdaq 100 futures were up 1.3%, while lower crude oil prices provided a contrast to the energy market conditions that had affected equities on Friday.
The previous session's losses had left the Nasdaq down 4.5% for the week, compared with a 2% decline in the S&P 500 and a 0.7% gain in the Dow.
The Federal Reserve's industrial production figures also showed faster-than-expected growth in September.
Investors continued to monitor technology sector valuations, energy prices and geopolitical developments ahead of the opening of regular US trading.

Partial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris , after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country. An overnight curfew will come into effect from 11pm until 6am local time, for Place ​de la Republique ⁠and the streets around ⁠Les Halles ​in Paris. Authorities earlier issued the country’s first curfew the northern city of Lille and surrounding cities of Douai, Wattignies and Denain. Curfews were also announced in the southern cities of Nice (specifically for minors) and central Lyon, while Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday.
It came after France’s PM, Sébastien Lecornu, said after an emergency cabinet meeting that he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said. Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.
France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting. Laurent Nuñez said there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations. Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than half a million and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years. Almost 2,400 arrests have been made.
Nuñez said he had offered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened” , but the president had refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”. “You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.
The original protests, led by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living , an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.

Ahead of leaving for a campaign rally in Wichita, Kansas, Donald Trump again claimed – without evidence – that the riots throughout France are due to mass migration .
“I told Emmanuel [Macron], you should close up your borders,” the US president said. “I’ve known him for probably eight or nine years. I told him as soon as I met him, I said, ‘you’re making a big mistake’. We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron ’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.
A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement .
Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.
Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.
The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier , said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.
On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen , said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.
The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.
Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”
Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.
Macron attends an agreement-signing ceremony with the emir of Kuwait on Monday. Photograph: Tessier Benoit/ABACA/Shutterstock It’s a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.
But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment .
It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.
Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.
Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.
Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis . In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.
But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946 . Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.
The markets are worried : France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.
The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.

The US state department has issued an alert warning Americans to avoid demonstration areas in major French cities after days of violent protests that have rocked the country.
The alert issued by the US embassy in Paris noted violent demonstrations on 17 October and the new curfews planned in cities including Lille and Paris.
“Avoid the areas of the demonstrations,” the warning said.
Justice minister Gérald Darmanin announced 2,513 people had been taken into custody and 67 people had been imprisoned since the violence that marred the demonstrations this weekend, Liberation reported.
Eleven people were arrested on Monday after disturbances at a shopping centre in Vaulx-en-Velin, near Lyon, BFMTV reported.
Here is the decree from the Paris police prefecture on the curfew which will be from 11 pm until 6am.
“The central median of the Place de la République” and “an area [...] delimited by the following squares and streets within it: Place Maurice-Quentin; Rue Berger from Place Maurice-Quentin to the corner of Boulevard Sébastopol; the section of Passage des Lingères that leads onto Rue Berger; Boulevard Sébastopol from the corner of Rue Berger to the corner of Allée André-Breton; Allée André-Breton.”
The prefecture clarifies that “residents who can prove, by any means, that their residence is located within the aforementioned areas, workers [...], members of the public emergency services, and shopkeepers are not subject to” the decree.
Demonstrations will also be prohibited from 8pm to 6am in other parts of the capital, such as Bastille, Châtelet, or near places of power like the Elysée, Matignon, the National Assembly and the Senate.
A curfew has also been announced in central Lyon , taking effect from Monday at 9pm local time until 6am on Tuesday.
Eric Ciotti , the mayor of the southern French city of Nice , has also issued a curfew “to protect the people of Nice” starting from Monday evening 9pm local time to 6am. The curfew will remain in effect each night until Sunday, and will only apply to minors, he said.
According to Libération, only certain areas of the city are affected: the city center, Old Nice, the Trachel district, and the Gare du Sud (southern train station).
French authorities have issued an overnight curfew, which will come into effect from 11pm until 6am local time , for Place ​de la Republique ⁠and the streets around ⁠Les Halles ​in Paris, according to Libération and France24.
The measure will apply to three categories of people: unaccompanied minors, people wearing personal protective equipment, and those concealing their faces.
Authorities had earlier issued the country’s first curfew to run for two days starting on Monday in the northern city of Lille and surrounding cities of Douai , Wattignies and Denain , France24 reported citing prime minister Sébastien Lecornu ’s office.
The prefect of the Nord department has issued an order imposing a curfew for minors starting at 8 p.m. local time in certain areas of the cities of Lille, Douai, Wattignies, and Denain.
“These orders are issued in close collaboration with the mayors concerned,” the prefecture said.
The Prime Minister’s office stated the measure is in effect for Monday and Tuesday nights, from 8pm to 6 am, Liberation reported.
In Coulaines, a town of 8,000 inhabitants near Le Mans, the mayor, Christophe Rouillon, also announced on Facebook that he would be implementing a curfew “in the evening for minors who go out alone ,” starting at 11 p.m. on Monday.
The right-wing mayor of a town in Maine-et-Loire has decided to fly the flags at the town hall at half-mast and remove the portrait of Emmanuel Macron following the demonstrations in France.
“I condemn in the strongest possible terms the violence and damage committed by those who flout our laws, vandalise our towns, and show contempt for the values ​​of the Republic,” Frédéric Mortier, the mayor of Longué-Jumelles, said.
“France cannot accept that some refuse common rules, reject the requirements of integration and challenge the authority of the State,” he continued.
The mayor added that he had also decided “to take down the portrait of the President of the Republic in the town hall”, explaining that the attitude of the head of state “in the face of this situation is unworthy of the gravity of the events and the expectations of our fellow citizens”.

The unrest included rioting, looting and violent clashes with outnumbered police in cities including Paris , Marseille and Limoges . François Gatel, Minister for Territorial Collectivities, told the National Assembly there will be “the mobilisation of an exceptional fund to support the reconstruction of public facilities.”
He added it will be “a one-stop shop to support disaster-stricken communities” to coordinate and facilitate the process. The minister also promised regulatory “flexibilities” to ease the work.
Shops were looted and public buildings were set ablaze in cities across France over the weekend, as nationwide protests turned violent.

Four police officers were injured and a police station was vandalised in the Garenne district of La Roche-sur-Yon by “around sixty individuals dressed in black and wearing balaclavas” who fired fireworks and other projectiles, Liberation reported.
Just before 1am on Monday morning, two motorbikes carrying one passenger each stopped at a traffic light on a backstreet near rue de Rivoli, one of central Paris’s busiest shopping streets.
“You’ve got to go where there are a lot of people, where they’ve done the shop windows,” said one motorbike rider to another. Minutes later 10 other men, their faces covered with ski balaclavas, came down the street on foot pursued by a police van.
People enter a ransacked Franprix store as clashes erupted at Place de la Republique following an unauthorised demonstration, central Paris. Photograph: Matthieu Rondel/AFP/Getty Images Soon after Emmanuel Macron’s televised speech on Sunday night telling the nation it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked”, groups of men looted shops in central Paris for hours for a second night running. Dozens of people attempted to smash windows near Les Halles shopping centre and grab goods. Others broke into an electrical shop in Belleville in the north of the city.
“Men were battering shop windows, trying to break in, then they were chased by police,” said a 73-year-old woman near Les Halles.
“There were different groups running everywhere with police chasing on foot or by car, and at the same time, some people were setting bins and bikes alight. The groups breaking into shops aren’t hostile to passersby so you’d see local residents walking down the street on their way home late at night, and masked teenagers running past in the other direction carrying looted goods. It’s so strange – it’s like two different universes in parallel worlds.”
“ It says a lot about society – it shows we have neglected our education system and that we’re living in a consumer society where all we say to our young people is: ‘buy, buy, buy’. In this type of extreme capitalism, some people don’t have enough money to buy all of this and so they attack.”

Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Map of Yemen Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
A person walks past bodies on the ground Bodies lie on the ground after the explosion at al-Alam camp in Yemen The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

items.content:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing , external in California.
US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.
The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.
Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.
On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".
Alfozan was scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

items.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
items.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
items.content:
By Michael Race ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Simon Jack ,Â  Business editor
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

items.summary: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profoundEurope live – latest updatesThe near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in Fra

Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the ‘deep anxiety’ of young people in his address to the nation but he has few fiscal options. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/Getty Images
Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the ‘deep anxiety’ of young people in his address to the nation but he has few fiscal options. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/Getty Images
Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound
The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.
Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured.
A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement .
French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots
Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.
Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.
The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.
On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.
The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.
Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”
Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.
It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.
But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment.
It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.
Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.
Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.
Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.
But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946 . Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.
French debt chart The markets are worried : France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.
The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.
Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections.
“Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde . “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.”

items.title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
items.summary: With $5 billion already deployed off its balance sheet, JPMorgan Chase is racing ahead on direct investments in defense tech, hardware and supply chains.
items.content:
JPMorgan's $5 billion bet on U.S. security; startups Castelion, Hadrian
JPMorgan Chase has deployed $5 billion into startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, halfway to its initial $10 billion goal.
The bank may exceed that target, co-President Doug Petno told CNBC.
JPMorgan has taken stakes in startups Hadrian, which builds automated factories for aerospace and defense firms, and Castelion, which is developing low-cost hypersonic missiles.
Separately, JPMorgan has financed and facilitated more than $230 billion in transactions in the initiative's first year, part of a broader goal of supporting $1.5 trillion in activity over a decade.
The head of JPMorgan Chase's new security and resiliency initiative, Todd Combs, then portfolio manager at Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seen at Berkshire Hathaway's shareholders meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, May 4, 2014.
JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative , the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.
The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview.
Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments , has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added.
Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion .
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago.
He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors , in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon.
The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries.
Troy Rohrbaugh and Douglas Petno, co-CEOs of Commercial & Investment Bank at JPMorganChase.
"There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said.
These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said.
In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder.
That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers.
"Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday.
"Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said.
JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.
Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.
In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.
That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine , a former co-head of investment banking.
JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada.
Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.
JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government's needs, he said.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov (R) meets with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (Back), in Tehran on October 19, 2026 [AFP]
Tehran, Iran – Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, to discuss the war with the United States and efforts to end it.
Lavrov landed in the Iranian capital on Monday afternoon on his first visit to Iran since February 2025.  Araghchi said talks with Lavrov had focused on regional developments, including the US-Israeli war on Iran.

list 3 of 3 Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy
He also called out Israel’s “dangerous expansion” in the region, which he blamed for the current hostilities.
“The existing insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz is a direct result of the military aggression by the US and [Israel] against Iran, and it is ongoing in different forms,” he said.
He added that Iran’s policy was to focus on diplomacy, as regional problems have “no military solution”.
“I believe Europe must also open its eyes to some truths,” Araghchi said. “Just like the Americans, the Europeans suffer from miscalculations and wrong interpretations, and have caused many wars and troubles around the world with their wrong policies.”
Meanwhile, Lavrov said Russia is committed to a 20-year strategic partnership agreement with Iran, which officially came into force on October 2. He said Russian specialists would gradually return to the Bushehr nuclear power plant after they left during the war.
The Russian foreign minister also linked restored navigation with protection for Iran against renewed attacks.
Lavrov held a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday. Pezeshkian said that he believes Russia shared “common views and approaches with Iran” when it came to his call for a world based on mutual respect.
Moscow said Lavrov’s trip was part of efforts to ease months of tension, since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28.
On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain, which was heavily targeted by Iran during the war, to participate in a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
He was urged by GCC members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels.
GCC chief Jasem Al-Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since the start of the war.
In the council’s closing statement, the six Arab countries said they wanted Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes, as well as its support for regional armed groups, to be included in future talks to end the war.
Nikita Smagin, an analyst and researcher on Iran and Russia’s role in the Middle East, said Lavrov’s trip reflects Moscow’s efforts to maintain working relations with all countries in the region.
He said Lavrov also wants to maintain Russia’s status as a mediator, despite the impact of the Ukraine war on its global reputation.
“The timing of visits to the Gulf monarchies and Iran, taking place almost simultaneously, is a deliberate signal: Moscow wants to show that it approaches relations with all these countries on broadly equal terms and is equally interested in cooperation with each of them,” Smagin said.
Lavrov told GCC ministers in Manama that the region was once again teetering on the brink of a full-scale war and Russia wanted to establish a regional architecture for “collective security”.
He said this could include combining initiatives from countries in the region, along with those put forward by Russia and China, with the aim of restoring maritime traffic and achieving lasting peace. The Russian foreign minister urged other regional states such as Iraq and Jordan, which have also been hit by Iranian strikes, to participate.
Lavrov expressed support for the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the US in June, which later collapsed, as a framework for reducing tension.
Iran has said it wants a return to that agreement, and for Washington to honour a finalised bilateral deal between Iran and Oman to manage territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. This has been opposed by the US, which has established its own route in the waterway for shipping.
Intelligence reports cited by US media said that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons.
But US President Donald Trump contradicted those reports last week, saying Moscow and Beijing would have “too much to lose” if they helped Iran.
Washington has also issued sanctions waivers for Russia in a bid to lower fuel prices driven up by the war against Iran.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (C) attends the 9th Joint Ministerial Meeting of the Strategic Dialogue between the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the Russian Federation in Manama on October 18, 2026. [Fadhel Madan/AFP] Mixed intentions
Russia’s position on the Iran war is somewhat unusual, said Smagin. It has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, as higher oil prices and the severe restrictions on Iranian oil reaching China all benefit Moscow.
“Russia and Iran have been competing primarily for the Chinese market, so China is now effectively forced to buy Russian oil at higher prices because Iranian supplies are largely unavailable,” he said.
Smagin added that Russia does not want the conflict to escalate further, as the consequences could be unpredictable, but its leverage over either Iran or the US to influence the course of the conflict remains limited.
Russia will continue to expand relations with Tehran, Smagin said, including through Caspian Sea trade, and limited military cooperation with Iran.
“These efforts appear to be aimed less at generating economic returns than at expanding Russia’s political influence over Iran and the course of events,” he said.
Military strikes by Iran and the US to wrest control of the waterway have continued, with the US midterm elections approaching on November 3 .
In comments to the media, Trump threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, to which Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi replied: “We have unfinished jobs too.”

items.title: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans - Vox
items.summary:
A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s airport is disrupting more than just air travel.
Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. AFP via Getty Images

items.content:
A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s airport is disrupting more than just air travel.
Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. AFP via Getty Images
As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital , Riyadh. The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities , and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure .
The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire. But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.
We’re running out of ways to get oil out of the Middle East
It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom , a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more. On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027 .
Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there?
They’re shooting from outside the country. They’re shooting from Yemen. The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades. They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government. They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards. Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.
They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen. They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise. And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia.
And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here?
If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.
And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia. You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.
Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis.
The Houthis have the world’s attention — and they won’t give it up
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure. How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been?
It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.
There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies. Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.
Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now- postponed ] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year. It draws a who’s who of global finance.
For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals.
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region. The stakes are really high for him right now?
They are. And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.
If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.
That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations. And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down. They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks. Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.
In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there. Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.
Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen.
What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused?
The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about. You can install additional air defenses there. You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic. There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.
As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport. You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.
Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options. One is you keep fighting. You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.
The other option is you cut a deal. You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire. That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia. I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.
If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option.
The US-Saudi relationship is too big to fail…for now
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment. Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet?
He has. He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen. And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that.
For the US to get involved in a bigger way, there are some practical constraints at the moment where a lot of American military assets are tied up in the Strait of Hormuz trying to keep that open, keep oil flowing through the Strait. And so the response from Trump has been disappointing for the Saudi Crown prince. The US is providing intelligence support. It’s helping on that front, but it is not directly getting involved in the war in Yemen.
Trump is coming for your credit card rewards. That’s good.

“We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” he said, warning of further repercussions “in the coming days and months”.
His remarks come amid continued instability in the Strait of Hormuz – a vital waterway for global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments – following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28, and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes across the region.
Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan industrial complex in March damaged facilities, with repairs expected to take several years.
“We were surprised,” Al Thani said when asked about the attack, adding that there had since been “a lot of discussion with Iran”.
He said Qatar had drawn lessons from the strikes, “to make sure that all of our assets will be protected from any unexpected attack”.
Al Thani also warned against imposing tolls on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
“Transit fees should not be applied,” he said, adding that uncertainty over the waterway would ultimately affect consumers worldwide.
Despite the attacks, Al Thani said Qatar continued to maintain contact with Tehran.
“We never stop our communication,” he said, adding that the two countries remained in touch at different levels despite their disagreements.
He described Qatar’s relationship with Iran before the attacks as one of trust, pointing to their shared offshore gasfield and longstanding economic interests.
Al Thani expressed hope that mediation efforts involving Qatar, Pakistan and Oman would help produce an agreement between the United States, Iran and other parties, including Israel.
He said a sustainable settlement would require broader regional dialogue involving Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, Pakistan and Turkiye, in consultation with international allies.
Al Thani also suggested developing economic ties with Iran to prevent future conflicts, citing cooperation between France and Germany following decades of hostilities.
“Iran is our neighbour. We need to find ways to live with them,” he said.
Al Thani also highlighted Qatar’s longstanding defence partnership with Washington, saying that “more than 90 percent” of attacks had been prevented through shared expertise and military capabilities developed over the past three to four decades.
He said Qatar was continuing to develop Al Udeid airbase, which hosts US forces and military personnel from other partner countries.
The base was itself targeted by Iran during the conflict, with Qatar reporting that it had shot down two Iranian warplanes during an attack in early March.
Al Thani also announced plans for a new regional defence partnership, saying Qatar was prioritising several aspects including air defence, counter-drone measures and cybersecurity.
“I’m happy to announce today also that soon we’re going to announce a new partnership,” he said, without naming the regional partners involved.
The deputy prime minister stressed that Qatar’s mediation efforts did not diminish its commitment to defending its territory.
“Mediation doesn’t mean that we should not be ready for any defensive action from our side,” he said.

Dow Jones, Nasdaq, S&P 500 preview: All eyes on Meta, Tesla, SpaceX earnings
Investing.com -- U.S. stocks fell Friday, closing out a mostly losing week as investors retreated from technology and AI-linked names while oil prices rose.

The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to 7,659.44, and the Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.14% to 26,140.03, with both indexes finishing below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The Cboe Volatility Index climbed above 22 for the first time in four months.
Semiconductor stocks were again at the center of the pullback, with the SOXX ETF falling 4.14%. Those losses, alongside broader weakness in AI-related shares, pulled the S&P 500 down about 2% for the week. The Nasdaq posted its worst weekly performance since June, down more than 4%, while the Dow managed a 0.7% weekly gain.
Despite the rout, the S&P 500 remains only about 2% below the record high it set earlier this month. Sectors that had lagged during last month's tech rally, including healthcare and consumer staples, posted solid gains over the week.
The recent stumble in the AI trade, which has powered much of the market's rally this year, faces a key test in the coming days as investors turn their attention to a wave of corporate earnings. Meta Platforms, one of the hyperscalers pouring billions into AI data center buildouts, headlines this week's reporting calendar.
Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »
Also set to report this week are chipmakers Lam Research and Texas Instruments, along with Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla. Netflix, consumer goods maker Procter & Gamble, and engine manufacturer GE Aerospace are also scheduled to report earnings.
Additionally, investors this week will parse a fresh batch of economic data, including housing starts and building permits, weekly jobless claims, and preliminary S&P Global PMI readings alongside the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey.
JPMorgan : "If bond yields are stabilizing, that will help equities, through allowing the cycle to look more sustainable, through reducing pressure on AI funding, as well as on consumer finances, and through reducing the drive for P/E compression. Indeed, during the most intense phase of yields spiking, forward P/E for AC World fell by 3 points, for SPX by 3 points and for Europe by 2 points. The multiple compression might not need to continue."
Goldman Sachs : "Equity prices should continue to rise as long as earnings grow. Positive but decelerating growth has historically been associated with positive but moderating S&P 500 returns. Equity returns in these environments have historically been driven by earnings growth rather than by valuation expansion. Within the market, a backdrop of positive but decelerating growth usually supports the outperformance of companies with secular growth over those with cyclical growth as well as stocks with price momentum, positive earnings revisions, and low volatility."
Morgan Stanley : "We favor quality in U.S. equities, but see recent volatility creating opportunity in higher-quality cyclicals given still-resilient growth. Capital Goods stands out, and has improving revision breadth."
Evercore ISI: "Last week's NDX selloff was the beginning of the price discovery process as a "perfect storm" for AI/Tech laid down "lines in the sand" that if crossed would transition the AI bull market into a correction, and if accompanied by a recession, could produce an equity bear market."
